accessibility.dialog.dismiss: Escape and a press on the backdrop call onClose. Put a visible way to close in the footer: Escape is a shortcut, and not everyone has it.
accessibility.dialog.name: The title names the dialog and the description describes it: write a title that says what the dialog is for.
accessibility.dialog.native: It is a native dialog opened as a modal: the focus stays inside it, the page behind is inert, and a screen reader announces a dialog.
accessibility.dialog.strings: Dialog has no text of its own. A close button that you put in the footer follows the language of the closest FormaProvider, through useFormaStrings().dialogClose.
accessibility.dialog.title: Dialogs
accessibility.errors.alert: The error is text under the field, announced with role="alert", and the border changes too: color is not the only signal.
accessibility.errors.changes: A Badge that changes while the page is open is not announced. If the change matters, tell the user in a live region, or in the text of the control that caused it.
accessibility.errors.linked: Field links the hint and the error to the control with aria-describedby, the error first, and sets aria-invalid.
accessibility.errors.title: Errors and announcements
accessibility.focus.dialog: A Dialog moves the focus inside when it opens, and back to the element that had it when it closes, so a keyboard user does not lose their place.
accessibility.focus.gone: If the element that opened a dialog is gone when it closes, nothing takes the focus back: move it yourself, to a place that makes sense, once the dialog has closed.
accessibility.focus.title: Focus
accessibility.focus.visible: The focus ring shows with the keyboard and is never removed. Keep it visible if you restyle a component.
accessibility.keyboard.loading: While it is loading, a Button stays in the tab order with aria-busy and aria-disabled, so a keyboard user does not lose their place.
accessibility.keyboard.native: The components start from the native element, and the keyboard comes with it: Button and IconButton are button elements, which Enter and Space activate, and Input is a native input.
accessibility.keyboard.reach: Every action has to be reachable with the keyboard. A disabled control leaves the tab order: use it only for an action that is not available at all.
accessibility.keyboard.title: Keyboard
accessibility.labels.badge: Color is never the only thing that says what a Badge means: write the status in its text, and use the tone to reinforce it.
accessibility.labels.field: Input has a visible label, linked to the control. A placeholder is not a label: it is gone once the user types.
accessibility.labels.icon: An icon alone needs IconButton, which requires a label and makes it the aria-label. Write what the action does, not what the icon looks like.
accessibility.labels.name: The content of a Button is its accessible name: write what the action does («Save draft»), not «Click here».
accessibility.labels.title: Names and labels
accessibility.lead: What the components do for the keyboard, the focus, names, errors and states, and what is still yours to do.
accessibility.next.body: Each reference repeats these obligations next to its examples, with the props that each one takes.
accessibility.next.title: Read them in each component
accessibility.states.color: State is never shown by color alone: loading changes the text and adds a spinner, and a disabled control is announced as unavailable.
accessibility.states.different: Loading, disabled and read-only are different states. Loading keeps the focus, disabled leaves the tab order, and a read-only Input keeps the focus and its value can be read, selected and sent.
accessibility.states.title: States
accessibility.tooltip.content: A Tooltip is a description, not a place for what the user needs: the page has to say the same thing without it, and the tooltip holds no controls.
accessibility.tooltip.describe: While it is open, the tooltip describes its trigger with aria-describedby. When it repeats the accessible name, as it does on an IconButton, set describe to false.
accessibility.tooltip.keyboard: It opens when the trigger receives the focus, and not only on hover. Escape closes it and the focus stays where it was.
accessibility.tooltip.title: Tooltips
accessibility.tooltip.trigger: The trigger has to take the focus (a button, a link, an input): a tooltip on an element that cannot be focused has no way in for the keyboard.
